title: What has to be done before 1.3.1 ships?

steps.path: The Next release list on the roadmap's front page
steps.headline: What is 1.3.1 for: going public, or going public plus a set of new features?
steps.today: 30 items are marked as blocking 1.3.1. They mix three kinds of work: things a public launch legally or practically needs, real bugs people would hit, and large new features or behind-the-scenes rewrites.
steps.problem: At 30 items, 1.3.1 has no finish line. Several of the biggest are on hold by your own decision (2026-09-18), so as tagged the release cannot ship until paused work restarts and finishes.
steps.proposal: Decide what kind of release it is. The next pages then sort each item into it or out of it. An item taken out of 1.3.1 stays on the roadmap; only its release tag goes.

options.label: Launch release
options.summary: About 11 items: signed installers, the Play listing, the legal paperwork, the Gemma licence notice, the safety-badge wording, the marketplace scan fix, the release tool fix, the local model forgetting your request, and three quick real-machine checks.
pros: A finish line you can see: most of it is paperwork and small fixes.
People can install it without scary security warnings, including from the Play Store.
New features then ship in later updates instead of waiting for all of them.
cons: The assistant-as-a-project idea and full project file search wait for a later release.

options.label: Launch plus features
options.summary: The launch items, plus whichever features you tick on page 3.
pros: New users meet the app with the features you think define it.
cons: Each feature added is weeks of design and building before the launch can happen.

options.label: Keep all 30
pros: Nothing is re-decided.
cons: Includes five rewrites you put on hold, so no ship date is possible until they restart.
Mixes developer tooling into what is meant to be a product release.

steps.intro: Five items change nothing you would see. They were tagged 1.3.1 and then paused on 2026-09-18.

steps.path: Roadmap: chat-data, local-models, native-harness, remote-access and user-interface
steps.headline: Should the five paused rewrites stop blocking 1.3.1 and ship whenever they are finished?
steps.today: Five cleanups each remove a duplicate copy of something: the phone and desktop features written twice, the settings screen written twice, the downloader written three times, one oversized conversation engine, and past-conversation lists that re-read far more than they need to. You paused all five on 2026-09-18 until other work lands.
steps.problem: They are marked as blocking the release but are also paused, so the release waits on work nobody is allowed to start yet. Only one is noticeable to users: the past-conversations list opening slowly on a big history.
steps.proposal: Yes: they keep their place and order on the roadmap and ship in whatever update follows their completion. No: 1.3.1 waits for all five. Don't know: nothing changes for now.
steps.risk: The duplicate copies keep drifting apart until the rewrites happen, so a change made on desktop can still be missed on the phone.

steps.intro: Tick the ones that must be in 1.3.1. The rest stay planned for a later update.

steps.headline: Which of these new features must be in 1.3.1 itself?
steps.today: Six features are tagged 1.3.1. None is built yet. Two have designs written, and the rest still need decisions from you first.
steps.problem: Each one is a real project. Kept in 1.3.1, they decide when the launch can happen.
steps.proposal: Ticked features stay 1.3.1 blockers. Unticked ones keep their place on the roadmap without a release date.

options.label: Full project search
options.summary: Finding files by name, and searching inside them, covers the whole project instead of stopping at 2,000 files or 200 matches.
pros: You said 'I just want everything to work' about exactly this.
The design is written.
cons: Four questions for you come first.

options.label: Assistant as a project
options.summary: The three linked ideas: a built-in 'Your Assistant' project, a proper incognito mode replacing 'No folder', and a YouCoded home for skills.
pros: It is the idea that explains the whole app to a new user.
'No folder' was shipped untested; this fixes it properly.
cons: Needs design decisions from you before anything is built.

options.label: Chat Search summaries
options.summary: Each past conversation gets a short summary saying whether it was resolved, open or abandoned.
pros: Makes the 'open' filter in search actually work.
cons: Optional and off by default, so most users would never see it.

options.label: Assistant searches marketplace
options.summary: The assistant can look for an existing plugin before building something itself.
pros: You called it a 1.3 blocker on 2026-09-05.

options.label: Parity program
options.summary: Everything still separating YouCoded's own assistant from a Claude Code session, as one ongoing program.
pros: Keeps the goal visible.
cons: An open-ended program, not one task. It can never be 'done' for a release.

steps.intro: Tick the ones that must be in 1.3.1. Unticked ones stay on the roadmap without a release date.

steps.path: Roadmap: dev-workspace, native-harness, user-interface and operations
steps.headline: Which of these smaller items must be done before 1.3.1 ships?
steps.today: Seven smaller items are tagged 1.3.1. Some are app fixes, some are about how releases are made, and one is about the website.
steps.problem: Several do not affect what a user of 1.3.1 gets, so they hold up the release for no user benefit.
steps.proposal: Ticked items stay 1.3.1 blockers. Unticked ones keep their place on the roadmap.

options.label: Forgotten approval
options.summary: After an 'Always allow', a command that looks covered still asks permission with no reason.
pros: Users see it: it reads as the app forgetting what they said.
Probably small.

options.label: Rest of error messages
options.summary: The 17 error messages that said something false are fixed. Six batches of smaller wording and action fixes remain.
pros: Every error offering an action is your own rule.
cons: Six batches: the false ones, the part that mattered most, are already gone.

options.label: Rest of hover hints
options.summary: Settings, the marketplace and project view still use the browser's plain hover hints.
pros: The app looks consistent everywhere.
cons: You chose on 2026-09-10 to convert them only when those screens are next changed.

options.label: Bug-fix release branches
options.summary: A way to ship a bug fix without also shipping every unfinished feature on the main line.
pros: Once the Play Store listing is live, quick fix releases become routine.
cons: Only matters after 1.3.1, for the update that follows it.

options.label: Faster test runs
options.summary: A nightly practice build and a way to re-run one test on one computer type.
pros: Cuts the hour-long waits you asked about on 2026-09-20.
cons: Developer tooling: nothing in the app changes.

options.label: Helper files pile up
options.summary: Files from helper agents are never deleted.
pros: Keeps the disk tidy.
cons: Cannot start until deleting a conversation exists at all.

options.label: Website demo blur
options.summary: The live demo on youcoded.ai goes blurry under some themes.
pros: Visible to every site visitor who tries the theme button.
cons: The website updates separately from app releases, so it can be fixed any day.

steps.path: The Next release list on the roadmap's front page
steps.headline: These eleven stay 1.3.1 blockers whatever else you pick.
steps.changed: Signed Windows and Mac installers; the Play Store listing; the LLC and trademark paperwork; Gemma's licence notice; 'Likely safe' badge wording; the marketplace scanning the wrong code; the release tool still expecting the archived repo; local models forgetting your request; and quick real-machine checks of the Linux update, the buddy on two screens, and the Mac 'Open Anyway' button.
steps.notice: Each one is either legally required, would break or embarrass a public release, or is a short check on a real machine. Most of the paperwork and signing is waiting on accounts in the LLC's name, which only you can open.

steps.intro: Neither needs to wait for the release.

steps.path: The download buttons on the website
steps.headline: Should the website's download buttons go back to giving visitors the finished release?
steps.today: Since 2026-09-03 the buttons on youcoded.ai hand out the newest build of any kind, beta included. That was on purpose: the only finished release then was May's 1.2.4. The code itself says to switch back once 1.3.0 ships.
steps.problem: 1.3.0 shipped on 2026-09-20, but the switch-back never happened. The newest build on GitHub is a test build, 1.3.1-beta.87, so every visitor downloading from the site gets a beta rather than 1.3.0.
steps.proposal: Yes: a few-line change to the website code, so the buttons give out the finished release. The betas stay published, and testers keep getting them through the app's beta setting. No: visitors keep getting betas.
steps.risk: None to people already using the app; it changes only which file a new visitor downloads. The site stores its answer for an hour, so a returning visitor may see the old link briefly.

steps.path: The badge on a plugin's listing
steps.headline: What should the marketplace badge say instead of 'Likely safe'?
steps.today: Plugins that pass our scan show a badge reading 'Likely safe'.
steps.problem: The scan only checks for leaked passwords and keys and for a correctly shaped package. It does not check whether the plugin does anything harmful. A public product cannot claim a safety check that never happened.
steps.proposal: Type the wording you want. The suggestion is 'No leaked secrets found'. Nothing else about the badge changes.
